title: HTTP APIs: reliable requests, retries, and pagination
sources: IETF RFC 9110 HTTP semantics and Retry-After; IETF RFC 6585 status 429; reviewed 2026-10-03
Python 3.14 urllib.request documentation; this lesson models policy and makes no library-specific retry API claim
masterChecklist: Sockets, HTTP concepts, REST APIs, requests, retries, idempotency, pagination, rate limits, error handling
whyItMatters: APIs fail in normal ways: timeouts, temporary errors, rate limits, and multi-page results. A reliable client makes those cases explicit instead of assuming every response succeeds.
simpleExplanation: HTTP uses requests and responses. Status codes communicate broad outcomes. A timeout limits waiting. Retry only operations that are safe to repeat or explicitly idempotent. Pagination means results arrive in pages; clients must follow the documented next-page mechanism rather than assume one response contains everything.
mentalModel: An API client is a courier: it needs an address, a delivery deadline, a rule for safe redelivery, and a way to request the next box when the shipment is split.
outcomes: Explain timeout, retry, idempotency, rate limit, and pagination.
Separate transport failure from application-level validation.

realWorldExample.scenario: A reporting tool collects paginated course records from an internal API.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: An unlimited wait freezes the tool. Retrying a non-idempotent payment-like write can duplicate an action. Ignoring a next-page cursor misses data.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Set timeouts, respect retry guidance and rate limits, use bounded retries with backoff, record safe diagnostics, and test each response category locally.

explanation: The example models response policy without calling a network.
200 means the request succeeded in this simplified example.
429 is commonly used for rate limiting; clients should follow documented server guidance.
A 5xx response can be temporary, but retry safety depends on the operation and API contract.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Try 200, 404, and 503. Explain why a write request needs an idempotency policy before automatic retry.

procedure: Read the API contract for authentication, pagination, errors, and rate limits.
Set an explicit timeout at the client boundary.
Classify whether the operation is safe to retry.
Use bounded retries and backoff only for documented transient cases.
Follow cursors or next links until pagination is complete, with a sensible maximum and diagnostics.

commonMistakes.why: Some writes can duplicate state or hide a permanent error.
commonMistakes.avoid: Retry only documented transient failures for safe/idempotent operations.

commonMistakes.why: A stalled connection can block the user indefinitely.
commonMistakes.avoid: Choose a timeout suitable for the user experience and service contract.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming one page is the complete dataset.
commonMistakes.avoid: Implement the documented next-page/cursor flow and test multiple pages.

lab.title: Design a local API response policy
lab.safety: This lab uses numeric response codes only; it does not call a network.
guidedSteps: Return a rate-limit wait action for 429.
Identify the 500–599 range as a possible transient case.
Return a clear error action for all other values.
checks: The function has no network dependency.
Rate limiting is distinct from general errors.
Retries are described as conditional, not automatic.
Unknown responses get a safe error path.
hints: return 'show a clear error; do not guess'
lab.solutionExplanation: The local policy is testable before an HTTP library and a real API boundary are introduced.
challenges: Find the bug: retry every non-200 status.
Experiment: add a response object later with a next-page cursor.
lab.testCode:
assert response_action(200)=='use response'
assert response_action(429)=='wait according to server guidance'
assert 'bounded retry' in response_action(503)
assert 'clear error' in response_action(404)
print('PASS: response action categories')

projectConnection.milestone: Define timeout, retry, rate-limit, and pagination policy before integrating a real client library.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: You can explain why retries require idempotency knowledge and how a paginated collection becomes complete.

assessment.question: Why set a timeout?
assessment.answer: To limit how long a client waits for a response.

assessment.question: What does idempotent mean for retries?
assessment.answer: Repeating the operation has the same intended effect as performing it once.

assessment.question: Why must a client handle pagination?
assessment.answer: A response may contain only part of the full result set.
assessment.explanation: The documented next-page mechanism retrieves remaining data.
